entities.title: What does a library do with extensions before there is a registry?
entities.summary: Obligation 7 says to fail closed on unknown critical extensions, but criticality comes from a registered extension definition, no library has an extension registry, and every library accepts extensions as an uninterpreted object.
entities.context: Spec §2: extension names are reverse-DNS or URI-qualified and MUST have a registered type definition, semantic operations and criticality behaviour; unknown critical extensions fail closed; unknown elective extensions MAY be retained as opaque but MUST NOT affect interpretation. Schema 1.0 types extensions as an open object, and the registry contract has no schema yet (OI-11). The C# and Java structural validators allow extensions as a top-level member without looking inside it; the Python validator applies the schema; the TypeScript validator checks only that it is an object. A library therefore cannot tell a critical extension from an elective one, and today keeps every extension as opaque data.

options.title: Treat every extension as unknown and critical until a registry exists
options.consequences: Any value carrying an extension is unsupported; safe, and rejects values that only carry elective metadata.

options.title: Keep extensions opaque, as today, and say so in each README
options.consequences: Values round-trip, but a critical extension that should change the meaning is silently ignored, against obligation 7.

options.title: Define a criticality marker in the wire format first
options.consequences: A minor specification change (utv/1.1) with a schema change; libraries can then fail closed on critical extensions alone.

blocks.description: Which part of the fail-closed obligation the libraries can meet.

origin.description: Found while documenting the TypeScript library (limitation extensions-not-interpreted), then checked in C# (UtvValidator), Java (Utv) and Python (the bundled schema).

entities.title: Which diagnostics does ctx.compare report when an overlap decides the order?
entities.summary: Comparing two zoned values that resolve to multiple orders gives one compare-level ambiguous diagnostic in C# and Java, and both sides' resolve diagnostics (ambiguous twice) in Python and TypeScript; docs/library-api.md does not say which is right.
entities.context: library-api §2 and §4 say ZonedIntent has no comparison operators and ctx.Compare returns Outcome<Ordering>, with ambiguous among the shared codes of §5, but not how many diagnostics compare reports or with which severity. Java was changed to report one ambiguous diagnostic (commit e0e80ff, Java: report one ambiguous diagnostic from TemporalContext.compare). Python's and TypeScript's TemporalContext.compare concatenate the diagnostics of resolving each side, so an ambiguous comparison reports ambiguous twice, and even a unique answer can carry the sides' diagnostics.

options.title: One compare-level diagnostic, as C# and Java do
options.consequences: Python and TypeScript change, and library-api §4 states it.

options.title: Each side's resolve diagnostics, as Python and TypeScript do
options.consequences: C# and Java change back, and library-api §4 states it; the caller can see which side was ambiguous.

origin.description: Found while documenting the Python and TypeScript libraries, against Java's commit e0e80ff.
